records.statement: Turing's lecture to the London Mathematical Society (20 February 1947) reports that it has been said that computing machines can only carry out the processes they are instructed to do, and argues that a machine whose instruction tables could modify themselves would be like a pupil who had added much by his own work.

time.note: Lecture date in the archive's title for AMT/B/1; the typescript itself is undated, as the dataset's records of it are dated.

engagement.rationale: Grants the statement only for machines used as slaves on jobs thought out in detail, and argues that a machine able to modify its own instruction tables would make progress its makers had not foreseen.

records.qualification: The lecture puts its case as a supposition (“Let us suppose we have set up a machine…”). The quoted report of the contested view names no one who held it. Proposed as U01's earliest located contesting text within this pack's searches.

evidence.passage: It has been said that computing machines can only carry out the processes that they are instructed to do.
evidence.note: The view the lecture goes on to contest.

evidence.passage: It would be like a pupil who had learnt much from his master, but had added much more by his own work.
evidence.note: Typed text; 'had' read where the typing is faint ('h d').

records.statement: Turing's lecture of 20 February 1947 says that when a machine with self-modifying instruction tables makes progress its makers had not foreseen, one is obliged to regard the machine as showing intelligence.
records.qualification: The earliest located non-fiction text on U02 in this pack; Erewhon (1872, fiction) is earlier. The lecture also answers the argument from Gödel's theorem against machine intelligence (pp. 23–24).

evidence.passage: When this happens I feel that one is obliged to regard the machine as showing intelligence.
evidence.note: A struck-out run of typed characters follows the sentence.

maintainerDecision.effect: Listed under the U02 headline as the earliest located non-fiction text.

records.statement: Turing's 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (Mind, October 1950) answers what it heads 'Lady Lovelace's Objection': it says the machines in question may in a sense have had the property, that machines take him by surprise with great frequency, and that the view that a machine can only do what we know how to order it to do appears strange in the face of learning machines.

engagement.rationale: Argues that Lovelace's evidence did not show the engine lacked the property, that a universal machine could be programmed to mimic one that has it, and that a learning machine's teacher is largely ignorant of what goes on inside it.

records.qualification: The section quotes Lovelace's statement, says that Hartree (1949) also quotes it, and notes (p. 459, note 1) that her statement does not contain the word 'only'. Proposed as the earliest located text using the proposition's usual name within this pack's searches; the use of a name is a separate role from contesting.

evidence.passage: It is quite possible that the machines in question had in a sense got this property.
A variant of Lady Lovelace's objection states that a machine can 'never do anything really new'.
evidence.note: Uses the name; the contesting follows ('Machines take me by surprise with great frequency').

evidence.passage: The view that 'the machine can only do what we know how to order it to do', appears strange in face of this.
evidence.note: A footnote marker follows the quoted view; the note reads that Lovelace's statement does not contain the word 'only'.

records.statement: Turing's 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950) states his belief that in about fifty years computers will play the imitation game well enough that an average interrogator will have no more than a 70 per cent chance of right identification after five minutes, and that by the end of the century one will be able to speak of machines thinking without expecting to be contradicted.
records.missing: The quoted sentences predict how well computers will play the imitation game and how educated usage will change; they do not state that a machine could think. Turing calls the original question too meaningless to deserve discussion. A separately located passage stating the claim, with its own locator, would be needed for an articulation.
records.qualification: In the same paragraph Turing calls the original question 'Can machines think?' 'too meaningless to deserve discussion'. Recorded as context after the cross-family check (item B8), which found that the prediction alone does not meet U02 as worded; the same-family audit (F7) had noted the same gap.

evidence.passage: Nevertheless I believe that at the end of the century the use of words and general educated opinion will have altered so much that one will be able to speak of machines thinking without expecting to be contradicted.

evidence.locator: Section 6, printed p. 442 (scan 10), the two sentences before the quoted one
evidence.passage: Turing believes that in about fifty years computers with a storage capacity of about 10^9 could be programmed to play the imitation game so well that an average interrogator would have no more than a 70 per cent chance of making the right identification after five minutes of questioning; he calls the original question too meaningless to deserve discussion.

crossFamily.result: corrected: articulates to bears on (context), as the checker found; quotation and paraphrase confirmed.

records.statement: Turing's talk 'Intelligent Machinery, a Heretical Theory' (c. 1951) sets out to question the commonplace 'You cannot make a machine to think for you', and says it seems probable that once the machine thinking method had started it would not take long to outstrip our feeble powers.

time.note: Catalogued c. 1951 by the King's College archive; no delivery date is attested. The year is approximate.

records.qualification: The record rests on the talk's stated purpose of questioning that a machine cannot be made to think, read with its expectation of a 'machine thinking method'; the contention on p. 2 is worded as simulation and is kept as context.

evidence.passage: "You cannot make a machine to think for you". This is a commonplace that is usually accepted without question. It will be the purpose of this paper to question it.
My contention is that machines can be constructed which will simulate the behaviour of the human mind very closely.
evidence.note: Context: worded as simulation, which U02's criterion alone does not count (audit F8).

evidence.passage: once the machine thinking method had started, it would not take long to outstrip our feeble powers.
evidence.note: The dataset paraphrases this sentence for its A1 and A4 context records.

records.statement: Turing's talk 'Intelligent Machinery, a Heretical Theory' (c. 1951) says that such machines will make mistakes at times and at times may make new and very interesting statements.

time.note: Catalogued c. 1951 by the King's College archive; no delivery date is attested. The year is approximate.

engagement.rationale: States that machines may make new statements, without here arguing against the premise that a machine does only what it is ordered to do.

records.qualification: A contention about machines the talk proposes to build; it says the machine's actual reaction to circumstances would prove it, if it can be proved at all.

evidence.passage: They will make mistakes at times, and at times they may make new and very interesting statements
evidence.note: The page break falls after the second 'at times'.

records.statement: Turing's talk 'Intelligent Machinery, a Heretical Theory' (c. 1951) says that a machine made sufficiently elaborate could give a very good account of itself for any range of tests, but that this would hardly be considered an adequate proof.

time.note: Catalogued c. 1951 by the King's College archive; no delivery date is attested. The year is approximate.

records.earliestLocatedFlag: Superseded: Jefferson's oration (BMJ, 1949-06-25) heads C1 under decision 5a. This record is a later C1 articulation.
records.qualification: The passage concerns a machine built to pass a fixed range of tests, which, the talk goes on, would give itself away by repeating the same mistakes. It does not name the imitation game. The talk's own view is that a machine's actual reaction to circumstances would prove its contention, if anything can.

evidence.locator: Typescript p. 3 (AMT/B/4/9, scan 9), paragraph beginning 'Let us go rather more carefully'
evidence.passage: It is clearly possible to produce a machine which would give a very good account of itself for any range of tests, if the machine were made sufficiently elaborate. However, this again would hardly be considered an adequate proof.

crossFamily.result: corrected: flag superseded by the checker-located Jefferson 1949; classification agreed.

records.statement: Turing's broadcast script 'Can Digital Computers Think?' (1951) quotes Lady Lovelace's statement as Hartree had quoted it, and says that he agrees with her dictum as far as it goes but that its validity depends on how digital computers are used rather than how they could be used.

time.note: Broadcast date in the archive catalogue.

engagement.rationale: Argues that the dictum describes how computers are used, not what they could do.

records.qualification: The script says the dictum describes well how digital computers are used at the time and will probably mainly be used for many years. It also notes that 'a different point of view' had already been put by Hartree (handwritten correction of 'The opposite').

evidence.passage: I agree with Lady Lovelace's dictum as far as it goes, but I believe that its validity depends on considering how digital computers are used rather than how they could be used.
evidence.note: 'are' and 'could be' are underlined in the typescript.

records.statement: Turing's broadcast script 'Can Digital Computers Think?' (1951) states his belief that digital computers could be used in such a manner that they could appropriately be described as brains.

time.note: Broadcast date in the archive catalogue.

records.qualification: The script's opening states the view Turing holds himself, 'that it is not altogether unreasonable to describe digital computers as brains'; its title asks whether they can think.

evidence.passage: In fact I believe that they could be used in such a manner that they could appropriately be described as brains.

records.statement: Turing's National Physical Laboratory report 'Intelligent Machinery' (1948) lists, among reasons for assuming that machinery cannot show intelligent behaviour, the view that any intelligence a machine shows is nothing but a reflection of its creator's, and answers that this view is like giving a teacher the credit for a pupil's discoveries.

time.note: Year on the report's title sheet.

engagement.rationale: Argues that a teacher would not claim the results of a pupil he had not foreseen, and that machines already exist where this arises in a small degree.

records.qualification: Recorded on the dated report (decision 10a); the undated typescript AMT/C/11 is its draft and carries the same two passages (pp. 2 and 4). On report p. 2 the objection's label is corrected by hand. Later than Turing's lecture of 1947, the earliest located contesting text.

maintainerDecision.effect: The text is recorded on the 1948 report, with the typescript as its draft; it appears as 1948.

evidence.passage: In so far as a machine can show intelligence this is to be regarded as nothing but a reflection of the intelligence of its creator.
evidence.note: Read here on the page image. The objection as the report states it.

evidence.locator: Report p. 2 (PDF page 4), paragraph beginning 'The view'
evidence.passage: that intelligence in machinery is merely a reflection of that of its creator is rather similar to the view that the credit for the discoveries of a pupil should be given to his teacher.
evidence.note: Read here on the page image; the label before these words is corrected by hand.

evidence.passage: The view (d) that intelligence in machinery is merely a reflection of that of its creator is rather similar to the view that the credit for the discoveries of a pupil should be given to his teacher.
evidence.note: The draft's wording (typescript AMT/C/11, n.d.); quoted in the earlier draft record, counted once.

crossFamily2.result: agreed: contests U01 (engages premise); the typescript AMT/C/11 keeps its own wording and label.

records.statement: Turing's National Physical Laboratory report 'Intelligent Machinery' (1948) gives, as a reason why people assume that machinery cannot show intelligent behaviour, an “unwillingness to admit the possibility that mankind can have any rivals in intellectual power”, and compares it with the possibility of being superseded by another animal species.

time.note: Year on the report's title sheet.

records.missing: A statement that machine intelligence will or could succeed people as the leading intelligence; the passage describes an attitude towards the possibility of rivals.
records.qualification: Turing calls objections (a) and (b) 'purely emotional' (report p. 2). Recorded on the dated report (decision 10a); the typescript AMT/C/11 is its draft and carries the same passage (p. 1).

maintainerDecision.effect: The text is recorded on the 1948 report, with the typescript as its draft.

evidence.passage: An unwillingness to admit the possibility that mankind can have any rivals in intellectual power.
evidence.note: Read here on the page image; the typescript (p. 1) has the same words.

crossFamily2.result: agreed: context; the report states an attitude, not a forecast of succession.

searchLog.searched: AMT/B/1 pp. 21–24; AMT/C/11 pp. 1–4; AMT/B/19 pp. 442–451 and 456–460; AMT/B/4 pp. 1–3; AMT/B/5 pp. 1–2, all read as page images. AMT/C/11 p. 1 quotes Dorothy Sayers (The Mind of the Maker, 1941): 'the nature of a machine is to do the same thing over and over again'.
searchLog.earliestNote: Turing's lecture of 1947 is the earliest located text contesting U01 in this pack; Lovelace (1843) is the earliest located articulation.
Turing 1947 is the earliest located non-fiction articulation; Butler (1863, satirical letter) the earliest located articulation and Erewhon (1872) the earliest located novel (decision 12a).
